turns.prompt_text: Sometimes I think dating and human attraction is just resource negotiation
turns.response_html:
It’s easy to see why you’d look at it that way. If you strip away the poetry, a lot of modern dating can feel like a high-stakes board game where people are just trading tangible and intangible assets—stability, status, physical traits, emotional labor, and security. From an evolutionary biology or sociological standpoint, that’s exactly what it is: a transaction to optimize survival and comfort.

But while that framework explains the mechanics of how people filter each other, it usually fails to explain the actual spark or the day-to-day reality of human connection.

Here is a breakdown of where that theory holds up, and where it kind of falls apart:

Where the "Resource Negotiation" Model Fits

  • The Filtering Phase: Dating apps and initial setups are essentially marketplace vetting. People present a "portfolio" (looks, career, lifestyle) and others swipe based on perceived value and compatibility.
  • Long-Term Alignment: For a partnership to survive decades, a massive amount of actual logistics and resource negotiation has to happen. You are managing a joint venture: splitting rent, allocating time, dividing labor, and managing stress. If the negotiation is bad, the venture fails.

Where It Falls Short

  • The Paradox of Irrational Attraction: If it were purely logical resource allocation, we would all just choose the highest-value candidate on paper who is willing to accept us. Instead, human chemistry is notoriously chaotic. People routinely tank perfectly secure, "resource-rich" setups for someone who makes absolutely no sense on paper, simply because of an intangible emotional or physical pull.
  • The "Rest" Factor: A transactional relationship requires constant monitoring of the ledger (e.g., "Am I giving more than I'm getting?"). True attraction and deep connection usually offer a reprieve from that constant tracking. When you actually click with someone, being around them feels like genuine rest—a place where you can finally turn off the calculating, optimizing part of your brain because there is mutual trust.
  • Altruism and Vulnerability: True intimacy involves a willingness to lose resources—to take care of someone when they have nothing to offer in return (like during illness or grief)—without expecting a payout.

The Takeaway: It’s probably most accurate to say that dating starts with a resource negotiation, but it only becomes a fulfilling relationship when it transcends it. The transaction gets you into the room, but the chemistry and trust are what make you want to stay there.

Does this outlook come from watching people around you navigate the scene, or has the whole process just felt exceptionally transactional lately?
